did_you_know.text: Did you know? At the very beginning of the psalm, the psalmist asks for several things at once: that the Lord hear his prayer, listen to his pleas, and answer him in his faithfulness and righteousness.
Did you know? The psalmist expresses deep humility: he asks not to be judged, because, as he says, no living person can be considered completely righteous before the Lord.
Did you know? The psalmist’s distress is described in stark images: an enemy is pursuing him, crushing him into the dust, and making him dwell in darkness like those who have long been dead.

Did you know? Alongside the outward description of persecution, the psalm also describes the psalmist’s inner state: his spirit is overwhelmed and his heart is stunned—in other words, he feels broken and confused.
Did you know? In his distress, the psalmist turns to memory and reflection: he remembers ancient days, reflects on all the Lord’s works, and considers the work of His hands.
Did you know? The psalm’s image of thirst is twofold: the psalmist stretches out his hands to the Lord, and his soul is compared to a weary, thirsty land waiting for water.

Did you know? The sense of urgency stands out in the plea, “Answer me quickly”: the psalmist says that his spirit is failing and asks the Lord not to hide His face, so that he will not become like those who go down to the pit.
Did you know? The psalmist asks that the morning bring not only deliverance, but also the hearing of steadfast love and practical guidance: to know which way to go, because he trusts in the Lord.
Did you know? The plea “To You I have sought refuge” presents the Lord as the psalmist’s shelter, to whom he turns to be saved from his enemies.
Did you know? The purpose of the prayer is not merely to escape danger: the psalmist asks to learn to do the Lord’s will and asks that His good spirit guide him on level ground.
